chapter_theme: The first seventeen poems of Nallanthuvanar's neythalkali: laments at the shore, most at evening, which the woman addresses as a cruel ruler, a hunter or Death, framed with political similes of just and weak kings; the friend reproaches the lord of the shore with the woman's pallor, slipping bangles and his broken assurances, and the woman speaks to her heart, to the sea, the anril and the flute, or tells of a dream; one poem lists the virtues to shame him, and one, a swing song, ends with his coming.

118.reading: The woman addresses the evening, which has come like the interval between a just king's going to heaven at the end of his reign and his successor's taking up the rule: it mocks her beauty, closed like a pond flower by thoughts of the man who left, fusses over hearts made weary by the herders' flute and the clamour of homing birds, yet cannot dim the beauty, sweet talk and opening smile of lovers who are together; unable to bear both the evening and the gossip, her heart wastes, while those who settled down without thinking of her rejoice.
118.nuance: Each stanza sets what evening does to the parted against what it cannot do to the united (கடிகல்லாய்), so the hour is cruel only by her circumstance. The opening political simile makes evening a lawless interregnum. The closing lines (22 to 25) are compressed and line 23 was repaired; the reading of the last line, the empty heart of the forgetful man rejoicing, is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the lament of a woman left at nightfall, the neythal situation; no shore is named

comparisons.tenor: the sun leaving the sky after its day's work, like a king who guarded lives going up to heaven
the moon rising to clear the darkness, like the successor who takes up the protection
evening, the uncertain interval between two reigns
her beauty closed up at evening
the lovers in union opening like buds on a branch
the sweet speech of women in union
the smile of women in union

119.reading: As the sun sets as if it had swallowed the day, darkness rises the colour of the discus-bearer, the moon comes up, flowers close as if their eyes had found sleep, trees bow their heads, buds open like smiles, bees hum like bamboo flutes, birds think of their young, cows crowd home longing for their calves, beasts go to their lairs and brahmins light the evening fire; those who call this hour evening are deluded, not knowing it is the hour that unwraps the life women keep bound up.
119.nuance: The whole catalogue is of homing and closing: birds, cows, beasts and the fire-priests all return to their own, which is the unspoken contrast with the absent man. The last word turns on காலை, which may mean the fixed hour (of ending) or the dawn; either way the poem denies that evening is merely evening.

thinai_evidence.note: evening as the hour that undoes women parted from their men, the lament of neythal

comparisons.tenor: the setting sun, as if it had swallowed the day
the moon rising as if to look at its own light
trees drooping their heads in sleep

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: a general statement; the speaker may be the woman or her friend

120.reading: Evening comes grim as Death grinning with the crescent for a tooth: darkness fills in like the heart of a pitiless man, the world dulls like the heart of one who must beg, the leaves close like the heart of one who hides from askers; the woman asks it whether it came, like a hunter aiming at a deer, like those who mock the beaten, like one who drives a spear into a burn, to torment those already suffering while their lover is away, and says this evening will vanish into darkness as a fierce enemy is driven off when a good king appears, once the lover hurries back.
120.nuance: Every simile is of cruelty to the already defeated: the begging, the burnt, the routed. The ending turns the political figure round: the lover's return is a good king's arrival that drives off the enemy who oppressed a weak reign (மெல்லியான் பருவத்து).

thinai_evidence.note: the woman's lament at evening for the man who left

comparisons.tenor: the world gone dull at dusk
the leaves of the trees closing
the evening, with the crescent in the red sky
evening tormenting those already in grief
evening deepening the pain of those already burnt
the cruel evening disappearing once the lover returns

121.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool shore, where at sunset the moon rises from the sea, birds go to roost and the dark backwater closes its flowers as if gone to bed, that since he turned away, the roaring waves are the only companion of the woman whose eyes swim with tears, the moving wind of the one whose body wastes, the lone heron pining for its mate of the one whose beauty fades like the moon at noon; as the returning wave takes back unharmed the fish the breaking wave left on the shore, his swift chariot could remove her pain.
121.nuance: The three companions she is left with are the shore's own sounds and creatures, each a fellow sufferer; the heron that pines for its mate (line 16) almost carries an implied sense, but it is named outright as her companion, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore and backwater at sunset

comparisons.tenor: the backwater gone quiet at evening with its flowers closed
his chariot coming to take away her pain

122.reading: Answering her friend, who says she sulked over small things without cause, wept and lost her beauty for a man who loves without grace, the woman says she knows he cannot see, understand or think of her while he keeps company with other women, yet when he tends her a little her shameless heart melts, rejoices and is calmed; so if her heart, washed by the love-sickness that hid at midnight, has gone over to him, her staying alive is a fine joke.
122.nuance: The three stanzas move the heart from melting to rejoicing to being calmed, each with a harsher name (நாண் இல், மருளி, அல்லல்); the closing irony is aimed at herself. No shore thing is named, and the situation of other women is marutham's, so my thinai differs from the colophon's neythal.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman who sulks at a man who keeps other women is the marutham situation

123.reading: On the fragrant shore where bees hum in the punnai and the great sea sleeps as if listening to song and lute, the woman asks her simple heart, which went in the helpless night, at the bewildering evening when sharks keep watch, and when the birds roost, to the man who caused her pain, whether it got to see him, embrace him, know him, and pities it for tossing day and night like the backwater's tide in longing for him.
123.nuance: The three questions (did you see him, embrace him, know him) climb in intimacy while the times of night move from darkness to evening to roosting, and each goes unanswered; the tide simile gives the heart's to-and-fro the shore's own rhythm.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore, sea and backwater at evening

comparisons.tenor: the great sea lying quiet amid the humming bees
her heart tossing back and forth in longing

124.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where the white waves ring the dune like the blue garment of Vishnu's milk-white elder brother, that since he left her while the town spread gossip, the woman hid her pain even from her friend, but could not hide her forehead yellowed with pallor, her wasted shoulders or her great eyes streaming; because she trusted the oath he swore by the god as one who would never part, she lost her beauty, so he should drive his horse-chariot and hasten his coming.
124.nuance: The refrain என்னையும் மறைத்தாள் மன் (she hid it even from me) makes the friend's evidence the stronger: what the woman would not say, her forehead, shoulders and eyes said for her. The oath by the god (தெய்வத்தின் தெளித்த) turns his leaving into a breach of faith.

comparisons.tenor: the sea and white waves around the dune

comparisons.vehicle: பீர் அலர் அணி கொண்ட பிறை நுதல்

comparisons.tenor: her eyes before they lost their beauty

125.reading: The friend tells the lord of strong horses that people who think 'no one saw' may hide the crooked deeds their own heart knows, but there is no witness closer than the heart, and though he knows this she comes to reproach him for having no love: he left untended the bond made when he drew patterns on her young breasts, the bond made when he dressed her in a leaf skirt, while she wept and wasted; let him pity her, for her bangles slip and the pallor will leave her crescent forehead if he marries her and does not leave.
125.nuance: She opens with a general maxim on the heart as witness before turning to the charge, so the reproach is built as a moral argument he cannot answer. The three tokens of the bond (the drawn தொய்யில், the leaf skirt, the waist-band of fine lines) are kalavu's gifts, now used as evidence. The last line asks for marriage (மணந்தனை விடினே).

thinai_evidence.note: the man is addressed as lord of the shore

126.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where at sunset the herons settle quietly on the dune like tridandi brahmins recalling the old sayings, that the woman takes the cry of the herons for the bell of his chariot, the scent of the backwater flowers for his garland, and in the long house, thinking of him, believes him on her shoulder and embraces him, then finds it was the birds, the flowers, a dream, and grieves; so let him yoke his chariot, that her face may shine again.
126.nuance: The three mistakes rise from sound to scent to touch, and the last, the embrace of a dream taken for waking (நனவு என), is the cruellest. Her body is held by longing as the herons are held by the old sayings they mutter.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore and backwater at sunset

comparisons.tenor: the herons settling silently on the dune

127.reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore, where bees hum in the njaazhal, punnai, kaithai and cherunthi and the sea rings the sand like the garland of the discus-bearer, whether it was for keeping his trysts on the white dune, for coming out to meet his chariot many days without a sign, and for meeting him at midnight on this lovely ford that he left her weeping, her bangles slipping and her forehead pale; let him give grace to end her pain, as the high wave hurries to shelter the adumbu creeper on its bank, lest the strong sun scorch it.
127.nuance: Each stanza sets her loyalty in the tryst (குறி) against his leaving, so the question 'was it for this?' turns her faithfulness into the charge against him. The closing image is stated with a marker and its tenor named (அருளினை), so it is an open comparison, not a hidden one.

comparisons.tenor: the sea ringing the patterned sand

comparisons.vehicle: ஓங்கு திரை விரைபு, தன் கரை அமல் அடும்பு அளித்தாஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the grace he should give to end her pain

128.reading: When her friend says she shines anew as if she had seen the lord of the shore, where the heron on the screwpine bent by the north wind calls all night heedless of their pain, the woman tells her that she saw the graceless man in a dream: she held him and demanded her beauty back, he embraced her and told her not to grieve, she wept that he forgot sleeping on her breast, he bowed to her feet saying she suffered like a peacock in a net, she struck him and he trembled asking his fault; and her precious life stopped at the brink, hoping that the man who came in a dream may come awake too.
128.nuance: The dream stages a full lovers' quarrel, demand, comfort, accusation, submission, blow and reconciliation, with every act prefixed by போலவும் (as if), so the poem keeps telling us none of it happened. The heron calling heedless in the night (line 5) is set against the man who comes only in dream.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore with screwpine and heron

comparisons.tenor: the heron that calls all night without pity
her new glow after the dream

129.reading: As the sun withdraws its rays like the creator gathering back all lives at the end of an age and the dark comes on like the weak reign that follows a king who ruled by the right way, the woman asks the roaring sea, the anril on the palmyra of the common and the little flute in the chill dark whether they too lament because someone loved them and left, and then asks the man to end the confusion of the one whose pain is now known to others, for leaving those who drank of him to break is crueller than a healer who cured a sickness smashing the medicine.
129.nuance: The three questions read the night's sounds as laments like her own; the anril, the bird that cannot live apart from its mate, is the apt second witness. The closing image of the healer who breaks his own cure is a charge, not a plea: he began the healing and now withholds it.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea and shore at evening

comparisons.vehicle: எம் போலக் காதல் செய்து அகன்றாரை உடையையோ
comparisons.tenor: the roaring sea, as a fellow sufferer

comparisons.vehicle: எம் போல இன் துணைப் பிரிந்தாரை உடையையோ
comparisons.tenor: the calling anril, as a fellow sufferer

comparisons.vehicle: எம் போல இனிய செய்து அகன்றாரை உடையையோ
comparisons.tenor: the plaintive flute, as a fellow sufferer

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she first addresses the sea, the anril and the flute, then turns to the man (பெரும)

130.reading: Evening comes desolate as the sun departs like the good age's wealth that died with a king who ruled without falsehood, and darkness spreads like the eyeless heart of a man grown old unlearned: as the priests lift the fire her helpless heart burns, as the backwater flowers close her heart closes in ruin, as the herders' flute plays her eyes grieve; yet the pallor of the woman suffering at sunset retreats wherever her lover touches her, as the vast army of a just king who guards his people goes wherever it is sent.
130.nuance: Each of the three evening acts (the lit fire, the closing flowers, the flute) is matched by one of her own, so the poem is built on juxtaposition. Both political similes come from the same theory of kingship: the good king's passing leaves darkness, and his army's obedience is the image of the lover's healing touch.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater flowers closing at sunset

comparisons.tenor: her pallor retreating wherever her lover touches

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the evening; the closing lines speak of her in the third person

131.reading: The friend pushes the woman on a swing hung from a screwpine, its frame made of shark's tusk tied with neythal fibre, and they take turns singing of the man who swore by the sea god and left: the shore where the crab hides in its hole at night, where the anril does not call at night lest the woman without her mate suffer, where the birds eat only fish killed by the waves and do not kill their prey, where the waves soothe the kaavi flower as he bows to appease sulking women; then the friend tells her that the man of the shore, who had been listening hidden, came and pushed the swing while she, thinking it was her friend, was bewildered.
131.nuance: The swing songs praise his shore in order to blame him: its creatures are gentler than he is. The birds that eat only fish the waves have killed (lines 31 to 33) imply the same contrast as the anril but are given as scene. The end is a comic recognition: the man comes to the swing in the friend's place, so the lament ends in a meeting. Line 18 has a gap in the source.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore with screwpine and neythal fibre

comparisons.vehicle: வாள் நிலா ஏய்க்கும் வயங்கு ஒளி எக்கர்

iraicchi.act: the anril pair hold back their night call, thinking the woman without her partner would suffer
iraicchi.sense: even the birds of his shore spare her at night, while the man who caused her pain stays away

132.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where birds rest with their mates on the dune and ships ring the harbour like the ordered camp of the three crowned kings, that her pallor, like a lamp in daylight, and her lost beauty like a mango's young leaves are the fruit of his 'do not fear' in the punnai grove; her slipping bangles, like a gem left unpolished, the gain of his 'trust me'; her hidden suffering, like a creeper shed of flowers, the yield of his promise on the dune; his going away while gossip spreads is as cruel as a god one worshipped as one's strength turning into an affliction.
132.nuance: Each stanza names one of his reassurances (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு, தெளி) and presents her loss as its 'fruit', 'gain' and 'yield', so the promise is turned into an account he must settle. The opening birds resting with their mates set off his leaving, but no second correspondence is stated, so it stays scene.

comparisons.tenor: the woman whose waist cannot bear its weight

comparisons.vehicle: வழிபட்ட தெய்வம்தான் வலி எனச் சார்ந்தார்கண் கழியும் நோய் கைம்மிக அணங்கு ஆகியது போல
comparisons.tenor: his leaving the woman who trusted him

133.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where the screwpine's hanging fruit is like the ascetic's water-pot hung on a tree and birds rest on it like blossoms, what the virtues are: support is helping the distressed, care is not leaving the one you joined, nature is acting with regard for others, love is not being angry with your own, wisdom is bearing the words of fools, firmness is not going back on your word, restraint is keeping secrets from others, justice is taking life without favour, patience is bearing with those who do not cherish you; knowing these, to enjoy her beauty and leave is to deny the cup to one who drinks sweet milk, so he should go and remove her grief.
133.nuance: The nine definitions sound general but each is aimed at him: போற்றுதல் is not leaving the one you joined, நிறை is the secrecy of kalavu that his leaving endangers, and முறை (taking life without favour) hints that he is as pitiless as a judge. The ascetic's pot in the opening simile prepares the moral register of the list.

comparisons.tenor: the birds resting on the screwpine

comparisons.vehicle: தீம் பால் உண்பவர் கொள் கலம் வரைதல்
comparisons.tenor: his leaving her after enjoying her beauty

134.reading: At the bewildering evening, when the sun sinks like the discus Krishna drove into a war elephant's forehead, the sea swells as if to see the night and the pond flowers close as if for sleep, the woman, thinking of the man who has not come, asks why the sea seems to take on grief, the sand to sink under her pain and the trees to close their leaves as if made of sorrow; then her grief leaves her quickly as the lovers hasten home, as a man whose ship broke in a shoreless sea is saved by a raft the waves bring.
134.nuance: The three questions (அஃது எவன் கொலோ) catch her reading her own grief into sea, sand and trees, and half doubting it. The final simile turns the sea from the image of her grief into the agent of rescue: the same waves bring the raft.

comparisons.tenor: the sea, as if grieving with her

comparisons.vehicle: கலம் சிதைந்து ஆழ்பவன் திரை தரப் புணை பெற்றுத், தீது இன்றி உய்ந்தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her grief ending as her lover returns

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she asks no one in particular; the close speaks of her in the third person

links.note: Kural 1229 says that when evening spreads the whole town is bewildered and suffers; Kalittokai 118's refrain says evening torments those parted but cannot dim (கடிகல்லாய்) the beauty, sweet speech and smile of lovers who are together.
links.teaches: Read beside the poem, the couplet's 'the whole town suffers' shows itself as the lonely woman's projection, since the kali poem insists evening harms only the parted, so the grief belongs to separation and not to the hour.

links.note: Kural 1221 tells the hour it is not evening but the time that eats the lives of the wedded; Kalittokai 119, after a long catalogue of dusk, says those who call it evening are deluded, not knowing it is the hour that unwraps women's lives.
links.teaches: The couplet compresses into one address the argument the kali poem builds through fifteen lines of homing birds, closing flowers and lit fires, so the Kural's 'not evening but a killing hour' is a summary of an established neythal rebuttal rather than a fresh conceit.

links.note: Both close on the same half-line, மாலை என்மனார் மயங்கியோரே; Kuruntokai 234 says that for the lonely even dawn and day are evening, Kalittokai 119 says that evening is really the hour that undoes women's lives.
links.teaches: The shared closing formula was a set rebuttal that could be turned two ways: the short poem stretches evening over the whole day, the long one narrows it to a killing hour, so 'those who call it evening are deluded' was a commonplace the poets argued with, not one poet's phrase.

links.note: Kural 1224: in the lover's absence evening comes like enemies to a killing field; Kalittokai 120 makes evening a hunter aiming at a deer, a mocker of the beaten, a man pushing a spear into a burn, and Death grinning with the crescent as its tooth.
links.teaches: The poem unfolds the couplet's single image of evening as executioner into a series of cruelties each aimed at someone already wounded, which shows that the Kural's 'like enemies' means an attack on the defenceless, not just a hostile arrival.

links.note: Both use the reign of a weak ruler (மெல்லியான் பருவம்) for nightfall: in 129 the confused dark comes like the weak reign after a just king; in 120 the cruel evening vanishes as the enemy of a weak reign is driven off when a good king appears, the lover's return.
links.teaches: The same poet places one political figure at both ends of the night, darkness arriving as misrule after a just king and lifting when a rightful king returns, so in these poems the absent lover stands in the place of the king and his coming restores order, not only pleasure.

links.note: Kural 1246 tells the heart its anger is false, since it cannot stay angry on seeing the man who ends quarrels by union; Kalittokai 122 has the woman, chided for sulking, say she knows he keeps other women, yet when he tends her a little her shameless heart melts and is calmed.
links.teaches: The kali poem supplies the setting the couplet leaves out, a friend mocking her sulks as causeless, so the Kural's confession that the heart's anger is false turns out to answer that reproach: she knows his fault fully, and her heart still gives way.

links.note: Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for following the man who left while lamenting his lack of grace; Kalittokai 123 asks the simple heart (மட நெஞ்சே) that went to him at night whether it saw, embraced or knew him, and pities it for tossing like the backwater tide.
links.teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's 'you go after him' looks like as an event, the heart's nightly journey met by three questions it cannot answer, so the Kural's rebuke of the foolish heart is the end of a scene in which the heart keeps coming back empty.

links.note: Kural 1235: the friend says the shoulders, bangles gone and old beauty faded, declare the cruel man's cruelty; Kalittokai 124: the friend tells the man the woman hid her pain even from her, but her pale forehead, wasted shoulders and streaming eyes could not hide it.
links.teaches: Together they show the body as a witness that overrides the woman's own silence: the poem adds that she tried to keep the pain even from her closest friend, so what the couplet calls the shoulders 'declaring' is a betrayal of her will to conceal, which the friend then turns against the man.

links.note: Kural 293: do not lie about what your own heart knows, for after the lie your heart burns you; Kalittokai 125 opens with the maxim that those who think no one saw may hide what their heart knows, but no witness is closer than the heart, and then charges the lover.
links.teaches: The akam friend turns the ethical maxim into a weapon of courtship: the Kural's inner witness, a general law of truthfulness, becomes the ground on which she charges a lover with knowing his own neglect, so the doctrine of conscience was already available to love poetry as rhetoric.

links.note: Kural 1218: when I sleep he is on my shoulder, when I wake he runs into my heart; Kalittokai 126: the friend says the woman, thinking of him, believes him on her shoulder (தோள் மேலாய்), embraces him as if awake, finds nothing and knows it was a dream.
links.teaches: The poem tells the couplet's moment from outside and counts its cost: what the Kural's woman offers as a defence of her lover (he never leaves me) the friend reports as the last of three daily delusions ending in grief, so the shoulder-dream is comfort in the first person and harm in the third.

links.note: Kural 1157: the bangles slipping past her wrist announce that the lord of the shore has left; Kalittokai 127: the friend tells the lord of the shore that her bangles slip (இறை வளை நெகிழ்ந்த) and asks him to give grace as the wave shelters the adumbu creeper.
links.teaches: The couplet has the bangles accuse the man to the woman herself; the poem has the friend carry the same evidence to the man's face and pair it with a remedy, so the slipping bangle moves from private proof of desertion to an argument for his return.

links.note: Kural 1213: my life lasts because I see in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Kalittokai 128: the woman tells of a dream in which she quarrelled with the man and he bowed at her feet, and says her life held at the brink hoping he would come awake too.
links.teaches: The poem shows the mechanism the couplet only asserts: the dream keeps her alive by letting her act out the quarrel and his submission and by feeding the hope of a real coming, so the Kural's 'my life lasts' rests on both satisfaction and expectation.

links.note: Kuruntokai 30 calls the dream of the lover's embrace a lying dream (பொய்க்கனா) that deceived her and left her wasted; Kalittokai 128 says the dream in which he came kept her life from going, in hope he may come awake. On a plain reading one treats the dream as deceit, the other as ground for hope.
links.teaches: The same dream of the lover is judged a cruel lie in one poem and the thing that keeps the woman alive in the other, so akam poets held no single view of dreams and used the dream's truth or falseness to mark whether hope survived.

links.note: Kural 1222 asks the bewildered evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; Kalittokai 129 asks the sea, the anril on the palmyra and the little flute in turn whether, like her, they have someone who loved and left them.
links.teaches: The poem shows the couplet's question as one move in a round of addresses to sea, bird and music, so the Kural's single address to evening reads as a compressed survival of a sung form in which each sound of nightfall is asked whether it too was abandoned.

links.note: Kural 1227: the sickness buds at morning and blooms at evening; Kalittokai 130: as the great backwater flowers close at evening, her heart closes in ruin (அழிவொடு கூம்பும்).
links.teaches: The two invert one flower image: the couplet makes the evening sickness bloom, the poem makes the heart shut with the evening flowers, so love's pain at dusk could be figured as opening or as closing, and the Kural's paradox depends on reversing the shore's ordinary evening closure.

links.note: Kural 1154: if the man who said 'do not fear' leaves, is the fault in those who trusted his word; Kalittokai 132: the friend asks the man whether the woman's pallor and lost beauty are not the fruit of his 'do not fear' (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு) and 'trust me' (தெளி) at their secret meetings.
links.teaches: The couplet's question of who bears the fault is answered in the poem by the friend, who reads each reassurance as the direct cause of a named loss, so the Kural's moral question has a speech situation behind it in which the promise is handed back to the man as a debt.

links.note: Kalittokai 133 defines அறிவு as bearing the words of fools (பேதையார் சொல் நோன்றல்) and பொறை as bearing with those who do not cherish you; Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths.
links.teaches: The same act is filed under different virtues: the kali friend calls forbearance toward fools wisdom and keeps patience for those who neglect you, while the Kural calls it strength, so this forbearance had no fixed place yet in the lists of virtues, standing under wisdom in one and strength in the other.

links.note: Kalittokai 133: justice (முறை) is taking life without favour (கண்ணோடாது உயிர் வௌவல்); Kural 541: justice is to examine, show favour to no one (கண்ணோடாது) and act after weighing.
links.teaches: Both define justice with the same word கண்ணோடாது, but the love poem gives its harshest form, taking life, in a list meant to shame a lover, so the definition of முறை as unbending punishment was common coin a friend could quote, and the Kural's procedural version tempers a stock definition centred on the death sentence.

links.note: Kural 1164: the sea of love is there but there is no raft of safety to cross it; Kalittokai 134: her grief ends as a man whose ship broke in a shoreless sea is saved by a raft the waves bring, the lovers hastening home. One says no raft exists, the other that the sea itself brings one.
links.teaches: The two use the same sea and raft with opposite outcomes, which shows that in love the raft is not something the sufferer can find for herself: the couplet's woman has none, and in the poem it arrives only with the beloved's return.

source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speakers, addressees and stages are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
kalittokai:118 line 23: a damaged word was replaced by the sangamtamil.com reading (flag repaired); the closing lines 22 to 25 are compressed and the reading is marked uncertain.
kalittokai:130 line 1 is not in the sangamtamil.com text (flag not_in_stc); the line, the opening of the definition of a just king, fits the simile of lines 3 and 4.
kalittokai:131 line 18 has a gap in the source (flag lacuna); the refrain's sense (the crab entering its hole on the moonlit dune) survives.
kalittokai:131 line 16, 132 line 18 and 134 line 11: the printed line number stands inside the line (lineation flags); the text is unaffected.
kalittokai:134 lines 14 and 18: ஃ restored from the old encoding (flag repaired).
